Mitosis versus meiosis, meiotic arrest, nondisjunction, premature separation, maternal-age effects, sex-chromosome errors, and paternal-age mutation risk.

Learning objectives

1. Describe aneuploidy and explain how it can arise during meiosis I, meiosis II, and early embryonic mitoses.
2. Relate aneuploidy mechanisms to male and female gametogenesis, explaining why female meiosis I is especially vulnerable overall while male meiosis I has a specific vulnerability to XY errors.
Why this Week 10 resource exists
The handout explicitly says it reviews undergraduate gametogenesis concepts needed for the Week 10 Early Embryonic Development lecture and for understanding trisomy 21 and other disorders of chromosome number.

1. Mitosis vs meiosis

Core distinction: mitosis preserves chromosome number; meiosis uses two divisions after one S phase to reduce chromosome number from 46 to 23.
Cropped handout diagram comparing mitosis with meiosis I and II.
FeatureMitosisMeiosis IMeiosis II
PurposeProduce genetically similar daughter cellsReduction divisionSeparate sister chromatids
S phase before division?YesYesNo
What lines up at metaphase?46 duplicated chromosomes individually23 tetrads of homologous duplicated chromosomes23 duplicated chromosomes individually
What separates?Sister chromatidsHomologous chromosomesSister chromatids
Centromeres split?YesNoYes

2. What makes meiosis I unique?

Meiosis I = synapsis + crossing over + independent assortment + homolog separation.

Synapsis

Maternal and paternal homologous duplicated chromosomes align along their lengths based on sequence homology.

Crossing over

Large homologous DNA segments are exchanged, producing recombined chromosomes.

Tetrads

Twenty-three tetrads line up at metaphase I, rather than 46 independent duplicated chromosomes.

Anaphase I

Crossovers resolve and homologous duplicated chromosomes separate. Sister chromatids stay together.

Exam trap
Meiosis I is the only division here where homologs separate while centromeres remain intact.

3. Male vs female meiosis

Male meiosis

  • Begins at puberty and continues through adult life.
  • Spermatogonial stem cells continue dividing.
  • One primary spermatocyte → 2 secondary spermatocytes → 4 spermatids.
  • Cytokinesis is symmetric, so all four products are similar in size.

Female meiosis

  • Oogonia proliferate during fetal life, then become primary oocytes.
  • Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I before birth.
  • Meiosis I resumes around ovulation.
  • Secondary oocyte arrests rapidly in metaphase II.
  • Fertilization triggers completion of meiosis II.
  • Cytokinesis is asymmetric, producing polar bodies.
Cropped handout summary: primary-oocyte arrest, ovulation, metaphase-II arrest, fertilization, and polar-body formation.
Why females are vulnerable
The handout emphasizes the extraordinary duration of prophase-I arrest — potentially decades — as a major setup for later cohesin/crossover deterioration and chromosome-segregation errors.

4. Aneuploidy: what it is

Aneuploidy = abnormal number of whole chromosomes. The handout uses 45 for monosomy and 47 for trisomy as the common whole-chromosome patterns.

Whole-chromosome aneuploidy

One chromosome is present once or three times instead of twice.

Partial aneuploidy

Only part of a chromosome is gained or lost.

Meiotic origin

Most common mechanisms involve segregation errors in meiosis I or II.

Early mitotic origin

Errors in early embryonic mitoses can produce somatic mosaicism, with a mixture of normal and aneuploid cells.

Mosaic severity
The handout states that severity in somatic mosaicism correlates with the proportion of cells carrying the abnormal chromosome number.

5. Two major mechanisms: non-separation vs premature separation

A. Non-separation / true nondisjunction

Cropped handout diagram contrasting nondisjunction of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I with nondisjunction of sister chromatids in meiosis II.
ErrorWhat fails to separate?Can occur in
Meiosis I nondisjunctionPaternal and maternal homologsMeiosis I
Meiosis II nondisjunctionSister chromatidsMeiosis II
Zygotic mitotic nondisjunctionSister chromatidsEarly embryo mitosis

B. Premature separation

Premature separation happens too early — before chromosomes are correctly aligned and supposed to segregate.

Premature homolog separation

Crossovers/cohesion holding the tetrad together break down in meiosis I, so maternal and paternal homologs align separately.

Premature sister-chromatid separation

Cohesins holding sister chromatids together fail before metaphase alignment; chromatids then segregate independently.

Cropped handout diagram showing how premature separation can produce balanced or unbalanced gametes.

6. Why aging oocytes are especially error-prone

Converging female-risk factors: long prophase-I arrest + cohesin decay + crossover instability + misaligned centromeres + weak spindle-assembly checkpoint.
Cropped handout comparison: young bivalent versus aged bivalent with loss of cohesin/crossover stability and abnormal sister-kinetochore behavior.

Cohesin and chiasmata

Cropped handout diagram: chiasmata help hold homologs together; cohesin helps hold sister chromatids and homologous chromosome structures together over time.
Normal separation
The handout describes separase as the enzyme that cleaves cohesins during normal chromosome separation: homologous chromosomes resolve in meiosis I, while sister chromatids separate in meiosis II.
Cropped handout diagram comparing normal anaphase-I resolution of tetrads with anaphase-II sister-chromatid separation.

Spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC)

Cropped handout diagram: a strong checkpoint delays anaphase until alignment is correct; a weak/absent checkpoint permits missegregation.
Female meiosis I
The handout says human oocytes have a relatively weak spindle-assembly “tensional” checkpoint. This makes progression through meiosis more permissive even when chromosome alignment is imperfect.

Trisomy 21 error distribution in the handout

Origin of errorApprox. proportion
Female meiosis I~68%
Female meiosis II~22%
Male meiosis I + II~6%
Early embryonic mitosis~4%
Mechanistic takeaway
The handout ties the high female-meiosis-I contribution to prolonged prophase I, loss of cohesins/crossovers over time, and the inability to replace meiosis-specific cohesins in an already-existing tetrad.

7. Autosomal vs sex-chromosome aneuploidy

PatternSource-derived distinction
Autosomal aneuploidy>80% due to defects in female meiosis, mostly meiosis I
Sex-chromosome aneuploidyRoughly equal rates of errors in male and female meiosis
Why male meiosis I matters for XY: X and Y chromosomes have limited homology and therefore synapse weakly, making them specifically susceptible to premature crossover resolution/separation.

Paternal age: different problem

Not mainly aneuploidy

The handout says there is no compelling association between aging men and increasing aneuploidy.

Point mutations

Repeated spermatogonial stem-cell mitoses accumulate new single-gene mutations.

Examples listed
Achondroplasia, multiple endocrine neoplasia, autism-spectrum risk, and schizophrenia are used to illustrate disorders associated with increasing paternal-age mutation burden.
